title: Maximum White Tiles Covered by a Carpet
statement:
Tiles sit at integer positions on a line. Each pair `tiles[i] = [l, r]` says that every tile at a position from `l` to `r` (both included) is white; the ranges never overlap, but they may come in any order. Tiles outside every range are not white.

You have one carpet that covers `carpetLen` consecutive positions and may be laid starting at any position. Return the largest number of white tiles the carpet can cover.
constraints: No two ranges in tiles overlap
notes:
## Intuition

Some best placement starts exactly at the left end of a white range: if the carpet starts on a non-white tile, or in the middle of a range, sliding it right until it starts at that range's left end loses nothing at the front and can only gain at the back. So only `n` starting points matter. Trying each one against every range is O(n²); after sorting, the ranges fully under the carpet form a window that only moves forward, so a sliding window keeps their total as the start advances.

## Approach

1. Sort `tiles` by left end.
2. For each `left`, lay the carpet from `tiles[left][0]` to `carpetEnd`.
3. Advance `right` over every range that ends by `carpetEnd`, adding its length to `covered`.
4. The range at `right` (if any) may stick out past the carpet; if it starts by `carpetEnd`, its covered part is `partial`.
5. Update `best` with `covered + partial`.
6. Before moving on, remove range `left` from `covered`. If it was never fully covered (`right === left`), just step `right` past it.

## Example 1, step by step

Sorted ranges: `[1,5] [10,11] [12,18] [20,25] [30,32]`, `carpetLen = 10`.

- `left = 0`: carpet `1..10`; `[1,5]` fits (`covered = 5`), `[10,11]` adds `partial = 1`; `best = 6`.
- `left = 1`: carpet `10..19`; `[10,11]` and `[12,18]` fit (`covered = 9`), `[20,25]` starts too late; `best = 9`.
- `left = 2`: carpet `12..21`; `covered = 7`, `partial = 2`, still 9.
- `left = 3` and `left = 4` cover 6 and 3. The answer is `9`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): the sort dominates; `left` and `right` each pass every range once.
- Space: O(1) beyond the sort.

## Pitfalls

- The input is not sorted (Example 2); sort by left end first.
- A carpet shorter than its first range covers no full range; without the `right++` step, the window would later count that range as covered.
- The carpet covers `carpetLen` tiles, so it ends at `start + carpetLen - 1`, not `start + carpetLen`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `left` | index of the range where the carpet starts |
| `carpetEnd` | last position the carpet covers |
| `right` | first range not fully under the carpet |
| `covered` | white tiles in ranges `left` to `right - 1`, all fully covered |
| `partial` | white tiles of range `right` that the carpet still reaches |
| `best` | most white tiles covered by any start so far |

narration.2: Sort the ranges by left end so the ranges under the carpet form a contiguous window.
narration.3: No placement has been tried yet.
narration.6: Try the carpet starting at the left end of each range in turn.
narration.7: The carpet covers carpetLen tiles, so its last tile is start + carpetLen - 1.
narration.8: Pull in every range that ends at or before the carpet's last tile.
narration.9: That whole range is under the carpet, so add its length.
narration.10: Move on to the next range.
narration.12: Range right, if any, is not fully covered; assume it adds nothing for now.
narration.13: Does the carpet still reach into range right?
narration.14: Count just the part of it from its left end to the carpet's end.
narration.16: Keep the best total of fully covered ranges plus the partial one.
narration.17: If range left was fully covered, it leaves the window as the start moves on.
narration.20: Otherwise range left was never in the window; step right past it so it is not counted later.
narration.23: Return the most white tiles any starting point covered.
